tldr: We propose ThinkWorld, a VLA framework that tokenizes both robot and human actions into a shared "Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD)" of discrete tokens and trains via reinforcement learning by imagining future environmental changes and matching them against reality, acquiring highly generalizable manipulation skills even from unannotated human videos.
hero_caption: Concept overview of ThinkWorld. Across human-robot embodiment gaps, a shared discrete motion token sequence (CoD) is defined. By predicting and comparing how the world will change as a result of that action, effective learning proceeds even from human videos without action labels. This achieves strong generalization to unseen environments and multi-stage task execution learned purely from human videos.
overview:
To enable robots to flexibly adapt to unseen environments and objects, the adoption of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrating vision, language, and action is rapidly accelerating. However, gathering real-world robot trajectory data is exceptionally labor-intensive, leading to an inevitable shortage of action diversity. Conversely, countless first-person human videos exist worldwide, covering rich environments and behaviors. Yet, because they lack direct robot control commands (action labels), they could not be directly used for imitation learning—a fundamental dilemma.

To bridge this gap, the authors focused on the insight that "even across different embodiments, the physical changes (dynamics) induced in the world by an action remain shared." First, end-effector motions of humans and robots are represented as a shared discrete motion token sequence termed "Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD)." The model is then prompted to "imagine" (predict) the visual features of the world 1 second into the future based on the CoD. Reinforcement learning (RL) is performed using the agreement between this prediction and the actual observed future frame in the video as a reward.

Through this design, even passive human videos with zero action labels can directly refine the reasoning space using "future state transitions" as supervisory signals. Across simulations (LIBERO) and real dual-arm robot experiments, the method demonstrated strong zero-shot generalization to unseen objects and layouts. Furthermore, even when the robot was only taught single primitive skills, it successfully chained them together to perform composite multi-stage tasks simply by watching human demonstrations.
contributions: Defined "Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD)," a shared discrete motion token representation bridging embodiment gaps between humans and robots, embedding action dynamics directly into the VLM reasoning space.
Proposed "Consequence-grounded RL," which rewards the prediction accuracy of future visual feature transitions induced by actions, enhancing reasoning abilities from action-unlabeled videos.

Demonstrated skill composition capabilities in real-robot evaluations: with only primitive actions trained on the robot, it autonomously chained the task sequences observed in human videos to complete complex tasks.

Achieved superior robustness under environmental and task distribution shifts on the simulation benchmark (LIBERO-PRO), significantly outperforming conventional world-model-integrated VLAs such as VLA-JEPA.

sections.heading: Unlocking the Goldmine of Human Videos: Reinforcing Action Reasoning via Future Prediction
sections.summary: While human videos are highly anticipated to alleviate data shortages in robot learning, their lack of direct control signals has constrained their utility. This paper introduces ThinkWorld, a VLA learning framework that refines action reasoning from unlabeled videos by using the consequences of actions on the environment (future prediction alignment) as rewards.
sections.details:
Endowing robots with general-purpose manipulation capabilities requires data spanning diverse tasks and environments. However, collecting trajectory data on physical robots via teleoperation is prohibitively expensive and hard to scale. First-person human videos have attracted widespread interest, but existing approaches face fundamental trade-offs.

The first approach involves Latent Action Models. These infer latent variables from frame-to-frame changes and treat them as actions. However, they easily get distracted by task-irrelevant information, such as camera movements and background visual changes. The second approach reconstructs explicit motion trajectories using hand pose estimation. Yet this relies on high-precision pose estimation and human-to-robot retargeting, severely limiting scalability.

A foundational truth is that "regardless of the embodiment, an action always produces changes in the world." Videos inherently capture these causal dynamics. Recent VLA models increasingly leverage intermediate reasoning tokens (Chain-of-Thought). This work takes that concept a step further: if intermediate reasoning tokens are grounded in physical world dynamics—specifically "how the action will alter the world"—they could serve as a shared action interface across humans and robots. This is the core motivation behind ThinkWorld.

sections.heading: Prior Explorations: Generalist Policies, Human Video Learning, and World Models
sections.summary: Existing reasoning VLAs remain limited to reinforcing reasoning within robot datasets, and human video methods rely on pose estimation or latent actions. Moreover, typical world models incur high computational overhead by generating rollouts at control time. ThinkWorld fundamentally differs by using future prediction alignment strictly as an RL reward during training to reinforce the reasoning space.
sections.details:
### Generalist Robot Policies and Reasoning VLAs
VLA models have advanced by incorporating knowledge from foundational Vision-Language Models (VLMs), yet pure imitation learning struggles to generalize beyond the training distribution. Recently, methods such as ThinkAct and MolmoAct introduce linguistic plans or spatial traces as intermediate thoughts. However, they only reinforce actions within robot demonstration data without grounding thoughts in the physical consequences of actions, thereby limiting generalization to unseen skills.

### Robot Policy Learning from Human Videos
To extract actions from human videos, methods like EgoScale map human interactions into robot control spaces, while approaches like LAPA learn discrete latent actions without supervision. However, the former imposes heavy retargeting burdens, and the latter easily confuses visual appearance changes with actions. ThinkWorld defines shared motion tokens and refines them based on the success of future prediction.

### World Models and Visual Prediction
World models exemplified by Dreamer train policies inside imagined future rollouts. Recent predictive VLAs forecast future pixels or latent features to guide control. In contrast, ThinkWorld does not use future predictions as direct control outputs or for test-time planning. It uniquely uses the alignment between imagined and actual futures as a reinforcement learning signal during training to shape internal VLM reasoning, allowing the prediction head to be detached at deployment for fast, low-latency execution.

sections.heading: How ThinkWorld Works: CoD Formulation and World Imagination Reinforcement Learning
sections.summary: We introduce "Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD)," tokenizing end-effector motion deltas to jointly train action generation and future feature prediction during SFT. Subsequently, candidate CoDs are sampled from unlabeled videos, and GRPO reinforcement learning is applied using the agreement between imagined and observed DINO future features as reward.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Problem Formulation
The input comprises a language instruction $l$, the current image observation $o_t$, an observation history $\mathbf{h}_t$, and proprioceptive states (joint or end-effector poses) $s_t$ for robots. The objective is to predict continuous robot action chunks $\mathbf{a}_t$. Rather than treating actions as raw control outputs, ThinkWorld formulates them as a "Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD)" $\mathbf{c}_t$ that reasons about how the environment evolves.

### 3.2 Chain-of-Dynamics: An Embodiment-Agnostic Reasoning Space
While joint angles are robot-specific, end-effector motion deltas can be shared across humans and robots. Normalized robot end-effector trajectories and human wrist trajectories $\mathbf{m}_t$ are converted into a discrete token sequence $\mathbf{c}_t^\star$ using a FAST-style discrete motion tokenizer $\mathcal{T}(\cdot)$ with a vocabulary size of 2048.

To predict the environmental changes induced by this CoD, learnable future queries $\mathbf{q}_{t+\Delta}$ are appended to the VLM. The model predicts the world state 1 second into physical time ($\Delta = 1$ s). Instead of raw RGB pixels, the prediction target is a feature map $\mathbf{z}_{t+\Delta}^\star$ extracted from a pretrained DINOv3 model. Using DINO features discards high-frequency textures and visual noise, focusing on spatial structure and state transitions. During SFT, the language modeling loss on the CoD and a distance loss $\operatorname{dist}(\cdot,\cdot)$ on future feature prediction are jointly optimized.

### 3.3 Scaling CoD Reasoning via World Imagination RL
SFT alone only teaches passive prediction conditioned on ground-truth CoDs. Therefore, the model samples multiple candidate CoDs, imagines the future state resulting from each candidate, and compares it with the actual observed future $o_{t+\Delta}$. The reward function uses feature similarity weighted toward dynamic patches with substantial change, preventing trivial rewards from static background alignment.

Optimization is performed via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), reinforcing the candidate CoDs that best predict the true future. A supervised replay loss is combined to retain the semantic motion grounding learned during SFT. Because this RL phase requires no action labels, abundant passive human videos and unlabeled robot videos can directly serve as training signals to scale reasoning.

captions.F2: ThinkWorld architecture and two-stage training pipeline. (a) SFT stage: human and robot motions are converted into shared discrete motion tokens (CoD), and DINO features 1 second ahead are predicted conditioned on CoD. (b) RL stage: multiple CoDs are sampled on unlabeled videos, and the VLM is updated via GRPO using the alignment between imagined and observed futures as reward.

sections.heading: Real-Robot and Simulation Validation: Generalization to Unseen Setups and Skill Composition
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted on a real dual-arm robot (Bimanual YAM) and simulators (LIBERO/LIBERO-PRO). ThinkWorld substantially outperformed baselines on OOD generalization across unseen colors, objects, and placements. It demonstrated skill composition from human videos and showed monotonic performance improvements as human video data scaled.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
The framework adopts Qwen3-VL-2B as the VLM backbone and MolmoAct2 as the action expert outputting continuous actions. The real-robot setup uses a bimanual YAM system operating at 15 Hz based on RGB streams (no depth) from one top-down head camera and two wrist cameras.

### 4.2 Real-World Generalization Under Distribution Shifts
Three tasks were evaluated on the real robot: cup hanging, color matching, and object sorting. Experiments included in-distribution (ID) setups and out-of-distribution (OOD) setups featuring novel colors, object categories, and unseen trajectories. Compared against Diffusion Policy, MolmoAct2, and LaWAM, all methods performed well in ID, but baselines plummeted to 20–40% in OOD settings. In contrast, ThinkWorld maintained high success rates of 80–100% (overall 100% ID, 86.7% OOD), proving the benefit of grounding reasoning in environmental consequences rather than surface visual cues.

### 4.3 Skill Composition from Human Videos
The robot was trained only on primitive skills ("open oven", "insert right item", "insert left item", "close oven") with zero composite demonstration data on the robot. Human videos demonstrating the continuous sequence "open $\rightarrow$ insert left item $\rightarrow$ close" were then provided. ThinkWorld successfully extracted the sequential structure from human video and completed the composite multi-stage task smoothly on the physical robot in a single attempt.

### 4.4 Simulation Evaluation (LIBERO / LIBERO-PRO)
On the challenging LIBERO-PRO benchmark featuring heavy environmental and task goal shifts, ThinkWorld attained an average success rate of 55.6%, outperforming world-model-integrated VLAs like VLA-JEPA. In particular, it reached 60.9% on environment shifts, surpassing VLA-JEPA by nearly 20 percentage points.

### 4.5 Analysis and Ablations
- **CoD Feature Representations**: t-SNE visualizations of the CoD hidden representations revealed distinct clustering by end-effector movement directions (up, down, left, right) rather than dataset sources (human vs. robot). This confirms that embodiment-agnostic motion dynamics were successfully learned.
- **Scaling Human Videos**: Keeping robot data fixed while increasing the proportion of human videos monotonically improved LIBERO-PRO success rates from 45.4% to 47.8%. This exceeded a robot-only control baseline with equivalent data volume, confirming that human video diversity directly enhances generalization.
- **Component Ablations**: Compared to the baseline (40.1%), performance steadily scaled: +future prediction reached 50.4%, +CoD reached 54.4%, and +world imagination RL achieved 55.6%.

captions.F3: Success rate comparison under distribution shifts (OOD) on the real dual-arm robot. While baselines degrade severely under OOD conditions with novel colors, objects, environments, and trajectories, ThinkWorld maintains remarkably high success rates (80–100%).
captions.F4: Demonstration of skill composition from human videos. Robot data only contains primitive skills ("open", "insert", "close"), but by observing continuous human videos, the real robot autonomously completed the multi-stage task "open -> insert left item -> close".
captions.F6: t-SNE visualization of CoD reasoning tokens. Clear clusters form based on end-effector motion direction (color) rather than dataset source (marker shape), demonstrating a unified motion dynamics space across human and robot embodiments.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Grounding Reasoning in Physical Consequences Expands Robot Learning
sections.summary: ThinkWorld establishes a novel paradigm that combines embodiment-agnostic dynamics reasoning (CoD) with world imagination reinforcement learning, eliciting generalizable manipulation skills from action-unlabeled videos.
sections.details: This work proposed ThinkWorld, a VLA framework grounding action reasoning in world state changes and reinforcing it using the agreement between imagined futures and actual observations. Because it can evaluate and enhance action quality purely through observed consequences, it unlocks massive amounts of passive first-person human videos directly for robot policy improvement. The strong generalization and skill composition demonstrated in both simulation and real-world experiments mark a significant milestone toward foundation models that transcend physical embodiments.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation Details, Closed-Loop Prediction, and Inference Efficiency
sections.summary: The appendix details the model architecture, training pipeline, additional evaluations on SimplerEnv, and inference efficiency. During deployment, the future prediction module is bypassed, maintaining a 15 Hz control frequency without extra computational delay.
sections.details:
### Model Architecture and Hyperparameters
The VLM backbone is Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct, with prediction targets derived from a $14 \times 14$ grid (1280 dimensions) of DINOv3 (ViT-H/16+). The VLM incorporates 64 learnable future queries that predict DINO features 1 second ahead via a Transformer decoder. The action expert follows MolmoAct2, consisting of a 36-block non-causal Transformer that generates action sequences using Flow Matching.

### Training and Real-Robot Deployment
SFT and RL pretraining utilized 128 and 64 NVIDIA H100 GPUs, respectively. During RL, $K=4$ candidate CoDs were sampled to balance computation. On physical hardware, a 15 Hz control frequency was maintained on a single RTX 3090. A major advantage is that during inference, the future prediction decoder is bypassed entirely, passing only internal VLM representations to the action expert, thus introducing zero inference latency typical of world model approaches.

### Additional Evaluations (SimplerEnv / LIBERO-Plus)
In SimplerEnv zero-shot evaluations without domain adaptation, ThinkWorld achieved a 46.51% success rate, with closed-loop rollouts exhibiting high visual feature alignment with target states. On the LIBERO-Plus benchmark containing sensor noise and lighting variations, it attained a 71.7% success rate, outperforming existing baselines like DreamVLA in robustness.

captions.F9: Bimanual YAM physical robot setup used in experiments. It comprises two arms and three RealSense D405 cameras (top-down head camera and dual wrist cameras, RGB only).

takeaways: Even without action labels, videos can serve as direct reinforcement learning rewards by treating the future environmental changes (state transitions) they show as ground truth.
Human-robot embodiment gaps can be resolved by converting end-effector delta motions into discrete "Chain-of-Dynamics" tokens, serving as a shared reasoning language.

Future prediction does not need to generate rollouts during real-robot inference; using it as an auxiliary task and reward during training provides strong generalization gains with zero inference latency.
Even when a robot is trained only on primitive skills, a shared reasoning space allows it to extract workflow structure from human videos and compose multi-stage skills.
limitations: Training results are reported on a single random seed, without exhaustive evaluation of checkpoint-to-checkpoint variance.
The future prediction horizon is fixed at 1 second; handling longer-term causal dependencies and variable-step horizons remains future work.
Because the tokenizer relies on end-effector delta motions, extending to tasks requiring whole-body coordination or bipedal locomotion remains an open challenge.
